data.text/markdown:
Math formulas compiled at runtime

This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) to compile and evaluate math expressions given as text, at runtime. MRPT wraps the exprtk library, which turns a string (from a simple formula to a small program with variables, if/else and loops) into an expression tree that is evaluated in C++. MRPT uses it, for example, to let users write formulas in configuration files. It uses two MRPT modules:
  • mrpt.expr: the expression compiler CRuntimeCompiledExpression.
  • mrpt.config: configuration files in memory (CConfigFileMemory), with @define variables and $eval{...} formulas.
Edit the formulas and move the sliders: everything below is recomputed.

1. Plot a formula

Write a formula of ||(x||) and three parameters ||(a||), ||(b||), ||(c||), controlled by the sliders. It may use the usual math functions (sin, exp, sqrt, abs, clamp, hypot, ...), the constant pi, conditionals, and even loops (statements are separated with ;, also after a closing }). Pick an example to start with.

data.text/markdown:
2. Small programs, and speed

The compiled expression is evaluated in C++, so a loop written inside the expression runs much faster than the same loop in pure Python. As a test, we approximate ||(\pi = \int_0^1 \frac{4}{1+x^2}\,dx||) with the midpoint rule and ||(n||) intervals, written as an exprtk program, as a Python loop, and with vectorized NumPy.

for (var i := 0; i < n; i += 1) {
  var x := (i + 0.5) / n;
  s += 4 / (1 + x^2);
};

data.text/markdown:
3. Formulas in configuration files

MRPT configuration files (INI format, used by many MRPT applications) are preprocessed when loaded: @define NAME value defines a variable, ${NAME} inserts its value, and $eval{...} evaluates a formula with this same expression engine. This keeps derived parameters consistent: change the wheel radius below and every speed limit follows. CConfigFileMemory parses the text, and read_double() returns the final values.
